opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really important question, and honestly one we think about a lot. With any LLM-driven evolutionary system you have several layers of stochasticity stacked on top of each other: the sampling from the language models themselves, the parent selection and island dynamics in the evolutionary loop, and then often noise in the evaluation itself. So you shouldn't expect two runs to produce the same program, and I don't think that's even the right notion of reproducibility here.

What we care about is whether the *process* reliably gets you to high-quality solutions. When we look at repeated runs with different seeds, the final discovered programs can look quite different structurally, but the performance they reach tends to land in a fairly consistent band. On something like circle packing, different runs find different constructions, but they converge to similar quality, often with a comparable number of samples. To me that's the meaningful kind of robustness: the search procedure is reliable even if the artifacts are diverse.

That said, I want to be careful not to oversell it. Some runs get lucky early, find a good stepping stone, and then exploit it quickly, while others wander for a while before hitting a productive direction. So there's real variance in the trajectory, and if you only report your best run you're giving a misleading picture. That's why I think the field needs to get much better about reporting distributions over seeds, median performance, sample-efficiency curves with confidence intervals, rather than a single headline number.

There's also a cost dimension. These runs aren't free, so doing ten or twenty seeds per task adds up, and a lot of work in this space ends up with only a handful of runs. Part of the motivation for making ShinkaEvolve open source and focusing on sample efficiency was exactly this: if each run is cheaper, people can afford to run more seeds and actually characterize the variance properly. And because the code is open, others can rerun things themselves and check whether our claims hold up, which is ultimately the strongest form of reproducibility you can have.

r001.rationale: The response names model sampling, evolutionary selection, and evaluation noise as stochastic sources, but does not mention server-side queuing or device scheduling.

r002.rationale: It says different constructions can reach similar quality on circle packing, but does not establish that this holds across many problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's a question I get a lot, and I think it's worth being really honest about it. The short answer is that reproducibility in the strict sense, meaning you set a seed and get the identical program out the other end, basically doesn't exist for a system like Shinka Evolve. And I'd argue that's not actually the right lens.

There are at least three sources of stochasticity stacked on top of each other. The first is the LLM itself. Even at temperature zero, the frontier models we're querying through APIs aren't deterministic, and we deliberately run at higher temperatures and sample across an ensemble of models, because that diversity is where a lot of the value comes from. The second is the evolutionary process. Which parents get selected, which islands migrate, which programs end up in the archive, all of that is sampled. And the third is the evaluation itself, because for things like the circle packing or the ALE-Bench tasks, there's noise in the fitness signal too.

So what we actually looked at is reproducibility at the level of outcomes rather than at the level of trajectories. If I run the circle packing experiment five times, do I consistently get to roughly the same fitness in roughly the same number of samples? And there the picture is quite good. The distribution of final scores is tight, and crucially the sample efficiency, which was our main claim, holds up across seeds. You don't see one magical run and four duds. What you do see is that the programs that get there are often qualitatively different. One run might find an SLSQP-based approach and another might find something more like a pattern-search with annealing, and both land in the same ballpark.

The place where it gets harder is the more open-ended tasks, like the mixture-of-experts load balancing loss discovery. There the variance is larger, and I think that's just the nature of searching a much bigger space with a much noisier signal. We tried to be upfront about that in the paper by reporting across multiple runs rather than cherry-picking the best one, and by releasing the full run logs and the final programs so people can inspect them.

And honestly, part of why we open-sourced the whole framework was exactly this. I'd much rather have people hammer on it, run it with different model backends, and tell us where the variance blows up, than make a claim about reproducibility that only holds on our particular setup with our particular API keys on a particular week. The models we're calling change under our feet. That's an uncomfortable reality for this whole field, not just for us, and I think the community needs to converge on reporting standards that take it seriously, things like reporting the number of independent runs, the spread, and the total LLM sample budget, rather than a single headline number.

r001.rationale: The response identifies stochasticity in LLM outputs, evolutionary sampling, and evaluation noise, but does not mention server-side queuing or device scheduling.

r002.rationale: It says different runs can find qualitatively different programs, such as SLSQP versus pattern search with annealing, that achieve scores in the same ballpark.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish two things: reproducing an individual result and reproducing the overall improvement across independent runs. An evolutionary search is stochastic, so I wouldn’t expect every run to discover the same solution or follow the same trajectory. The more meaningful question is whether, under the same conditions and compute budget, it consistently produces improvements.

To establish that, you’d want multiple independent runs and the distribution of outcomes, rather than just the best result. You’d also need to keep the evaluation setup fixed and track the sources of randomness, including model sampling. The conversation here doesn’t give us those repeated-run measurements, so I can’t make a quantitative claim about how reproducible Shinka Evolve’s results are.

r001.rationale: It mentions stochastic search and model sampling, but does not identify server-side queuing or device scheduling as sources of stochasticity.

r002.rationale: It does not state that distinct programs can achieve similar scores; it discusses different runs finding different solutions generally.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish reproducing a particular run from reproducing the overall result. In an evolutionary search, you shouldn’t expect every run to follow the same trajectory or discover the same program. The more useful question is whether independent runs reliably produce improvements under the same evaluation conditions.

To establish that, you’d want multiple runs with different seeds, a fixed search budget, and the distribution of outcomes—not just the best run. There can also be variability in the model generating candidates and in the evaluation itself. I don’t have those repeated-run measurements in this conversation, so I wouldn’t claim a specific level of reproducibility for Shinka Evolve. That’s something you have to demonstrate empirically.
